claim: 10.45% (551) of ORF-Ts showed a >threefold increase in transcription in GAL relative to GLU.
source: 10.45% (551) of ORF-Ts (open reading frame—transcripts) showed a >threefold increase and 9.99% (527) showed a >threefold decrease in transcription in GAL relative to GLU (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NET-seq experimental data comparing transcription in glucose vs galactose conditions, as stated in the manuscript text.

claim: 9.99% (527) of ORF-Ts showed a >threefold decrease in transcription in GAL relative to GLU.
source: 10.45% (551) of ORF-Ts (open reading frame—transcripts) showed a >threefold increase and 9.99% (527) showed a >threefold decrease in transcription in GAL relative to GLU (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NET-seq experimental data comparing transcription in glucose vs galactose conditions.

claim: For the majority (≈88%) of genes, the change in transcript levels on the GLU to GAL shift reflects altered transcription rather than altered transcript stability.
source: By comparing the NET-seq output with a microarray of Poly(A)+ RNA, we show that for the majority (≈88%) of genes, the change in transcript levels on the GLU to GAL shift reflects altered transcription rather than altered transcript stability (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of NET-seq data (nascent transcription) with microarray data (steady-state RNA levels).

claim: Genes whose transcription decreases in GAL are enriched (467; 88.6% p < 1x10−5) for OX phase genes that are mainly involved in ribosome biosynthesis and growth.
source: The genes whose transcription decreases in GAL are enriched (467; 88.6% p < 1x10−5) for OX phase genes that are mainly involved in ribosome biosynthesis and growth (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis and YMC phase classification of genes showing decreased transcription in galactose, with statistical significance indicated.

claim: For genes whose transcription increases in GAL, there is significant enrichment (392; 71.1%, p < 1 × 10−5) for genes whose expression peaks in the reductive charging phase (RC) of the YMC.
source: By contrast, for genes whose transcription increases in GAL, there is significant enrichment (392; 71.1%, p < 1 × 10−5) for genes whose expression peaks in the reductive charging phase (RC) of the YMC (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis and YMC phase classification with statistical significance.

claim: 33.1% (891) of the 2691 annotated OX- and RC-regulated genes show >threefold change on the GLU to GAL shift.
source: 33.1% (891) of the 2691 annotated OX- and RC-regulated genes also show >threefold change on the GLU to GAL shift, supporting a shared regulatory mechanism between the YMC and the GLU to GAL shift (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of overlap between YMC-regulated genes and genes showing transcriptional changes during carbon source shift.

claim: Antisense transcription reads increase in GAL compared to GLU.
source: These include antisense transcription reads (to ORF-Ts), which increase in GAL compared to GLU (Figure 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by NET-seq data showing strand-specific transcription reads.

claim: 25.7% of the 1772 annotated non-coding transcripts (SUTs or CUTs) show >threefold change in transcription on the GLU to GAL shift.
source: 25.7% of the 1772 annotated non-coding transcripts, the stable unannotated transcripts (SUTs), or cryptic unstable transcripts (CUTs), which show >threefold change in transcription on the GLU to GAL shift (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by NET-seq analysis of non-coding transcripts during carbon source shift.

claim: Pairs of ORF-Ts in the convergent orientation occur more often than expected.
source: In summary, pairs of ORF-Ts in the convergent orientation occur more often than expected, while tandemly arranged ORF-Ts occur less often than expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by computer simulation comparing observed gene arrangements to random shuffling.

claim: Tandemly arranged ORF-Ts occur less often than expected.
source: In summary, pairs of ORF-Ts in the convergent orientation occur more often than expected, while tandemly arranged ORF-Ts occur less often than expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by computer simulation comparing observed gene arrangements to random shuffling.

claim: YMC genes are clustered, with 503 (16.9%) YMC genes flanked by non-cycling genes, 1431 (48.4%) with a single adjacent YMC partner either upstream or downstream and 1023 (34.5%) with a neighbouring cycling gene both upstream and downstream.
source: YMC genes are clustered, with 503 (16.9%) YMC genes flanked by non-cycling genes, 1431 (48.4%) with a single adjacent YMC partner either upstream or downstream and 1023 (34.5%) with a neighbouring cycling gene both upstream and downstream.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of YMC gene organization in the genome.

claim: ORF-T clusters are more likely to show increased transcription in GLU or GAL than expected.
source: Compared to more isolated genes, ORF-T clusters are more likely to show increased transcription in GLU or GAL than expected, suggesting that clustering is associated with some aspect of their regulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulation comparing clustered vs isolated genes.

claim: ORF-Ts flanked by annotated SUTs or CUTs occur more often than expected.
source: In addition, ORF-Ts flanked by annotated SUTs or CUTs (in any orientation) occur more often than expected and show a twofold to fourfold higher median expression upon change from GLU to GAL than the average median expression obtained through the simulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulation analysis.

claim: ORF-Ts flanked by SUTs or CUTs show a twofold to fourfold higher median expression upon change from GLU to GAL than the average median expression obtained through simulations.
source: In addition, ORF-Ts flanked by annotated SUTs or CUTs (in any orientation) occur more often than expected and show a twofold to fourfold higher median expression upon change from GLU to GAL than the average median expression obtained through the simulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulation comparing expression levels.

claim: CUTs and SUTs play a role in modulating ORF-T transcription, particularly on environmental change.
source: This is consistent with CUTs and SUTs playing a role in modulating ORF-T transcription, particularly on environmental change (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by the observed correlation between CUT/SUT presence and ORF-T expression changes, and is also supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Convergent overlapping arrangements occur three times more frequently than expected.
source: Convergent overlapping arrangements occur three times more frequently than expected, whether the feature is a non-coding transcript (NC) such as a SUT or a CUT, or an ORF-T, with a median overlap of 92 bp for convergent ORF-Ts and 462 bp for ORF-Ts with non-coding transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulation analysis of genome organization.

claim: The median overlap is 92 bp for convergent ORF-Ts.
source: Convergent overlapping arrangements occur three times more frequently than expected, whether the feature is a non-coding transcript (NC) such as a SUT or a CUT, or an ORF-T, with a median overlap of 92 bp for convergent ORF-Ts and 462 bp for ORF-Ts with non-coding transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurement of overlapping regions in the genome.

claim: The median overlap is 462 bp for ORF-Ts with non-coding transcripts.
source: Convergent overlapping arrangements occur three times more frequently than expected, whether the feature is a non-coding transcript (NC) such as a SUT or a CUT, or an ORF-T, with a median overlap of 92 bp for convergent ORF-Ts and 462 bp for ORF-Ts with non-coding transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurement of overlapping regions in the genome.

claim: OX genes show higher than expected transcriptional rates in GLU, but not in GAL, regardless of the nature or orientation of the upstream feature.
source: OX genes, regardless of the nature (OX or RC) or orientation (divergent or tandem) of the upstream feature showed higher than expected transcriptional rates in GLU, but not in GAL, suggesting they are activated in GLU but not repressed in GAL.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of transcription rates in different carbon sources.

claim: OX genes are activated in GLU but not repressed in GAL.
source: OX genes, regardless of the nature (OX or RC) or orientation (divergent or tandem) of the upstream feature showed higher than expected transcriptional rates in GLU, but not in GAL, suggesting they are activated in GLU but not repressed in GAL.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OX genes show high transcription in GLU but not low transcription in GAL.

claim: RC genes are more likely to show higher than expected transcriptional rates in GAL.
source: Similarly, RC genes are more likely to show higher than expected transcriptional rates in GAL.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of transcription rates.

claim: When an RC gene has a divergent upstream OX gene, the transcription of the downstream RC pair is not enriched or depleted in GLU.
source: With a divergent upstream OX gene, the transcription of the downstream RC pair is not enriched or depleted in GLU.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of gene pair behavior.

claim: If the OX gene is in tandem with an RC gene, the RC gene is repressed in GLU.
source: However, if the OX gene is in tandem, the RC gene is repressed in GLU.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of tandem gene pairs.

claim: At the OX.RC tandem pair, transcription of the OX gene is mediating transcriptional interference and repressing the transcription of the RC gene in GLU.
source: This raises the possibility that at the OX.RC tandem pair, transcription of the OX gene is mediating transcriptional interference and repressing the transcription of the RC gene in GLU.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that tandem OX-RC pairs show RC repression in GLU.

claim: The downstream gene in a tandem RC.RC pair shows significant repression in glucose.
source: We note that the downstream gene in a tandem RC.RC pair also shows significant repression in glucose.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of RC.RC tandem pairs.

claim: Common features of regulated tandem clusters include reciprocal transcription in GLU and GAL, reciprocally cycling transcripts in the YMC, reciprocal AS transcription to OX genes, di-cistronic transcripts, and/or antisense transcripts spanning promoters.
source: Common features of the regulated tandem clusters include reciprocal transcription in GLU and GAL, reciprocally cycling transcripts in the YMC, reciprocal AS transcription to OX genes, di-cistronic transcripts, and/or antisense transcripts spanning promoters that could mediate temporal transcriptional interference and thus facilitate cycling transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multiple gene clusters showing these features.

claim: BAT2 transcripts peak in the RC phase of the YMC and in GAL.
source: BAT2 transcripts peak in the RC phase of the YMC and in GAL, reciprocal to HMS2 sense transcripts, which peak in the OX phase of the YMC and in GLU (Figure 1F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by YMC expression profiles and NET-seq data shown in figures.

claim: HMS2 sense transcripts peak in the OX phase of the YMC and in GLU.
source: BAT2 transcripts peak in the RC phase of the YMC and in GAL, reciprocal to HMS2 sense transcripts, which peak in the OX phase of the YMC and in GLU (Figure 1F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by YMC expression profiles and NET-seq data shown in figures.

claim: There is a reciprocal relationship between HMS2 and its antisense SUT650.
source: Interestingly, there is also a reciprocal relationship between HMS2 and its antisense SUT650 (transcripts A and B respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data showing opposite patterns for HMS2 and SUT650.

claim: No examples of FISH signals for both HMS2 and SUT650 at the site of transcription in the nucleus are observed in either GLU or GAL.
source: In multiple analyses, no examples of FISH signals for both HMS2 and SUT650 at the site of transcription in the nucleus are observed in either GLU or GAL.
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-labelled RNA FISH experiments.

claim: 35.5 ± 7.9% of the cells contained both HMS2 and SUT650 transcripts in GLU.
source: 35.5 ± 7.9% of the cells contained both transcripts in GLU, 22.8 ± 10.5% of all cells lacked both the SUT650 and HMS2 sense transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA FISH analysis.

claim: 22.8 ± 10.5% of all cells lacked both the SUT650 and HMS2 sense transcripts.
source: 35.5 ± 7.9% of the cells contained both transcripts in GLU, 22.8 ± 10.5% of all cells lacked both the SUT650 and HMS2 sense transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA FISH analysis.

claim: More cells contained antisense transcripts in GAL than GLU.
source: For cells containing a single type of transcript, more cells contained antisense transcripts in GAL than GLU while more cells contained sense transcripts in GLU than GAL (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA FISH analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: More cells contained sense transcripts in GLU than GAL.
source: For cells containing a single type of transcript, more cells contained antisense transcripts in GAL than GLU while more cells contained sense transcripts in GLU than GAL (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA FISH analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The increase in levels of SUT650 transcripts in GAL reflects an increase in the number of cells expressing SUT650 and a concomitant decrease in the number of cells expressing HMS2, rather than a change in the levels of transcripts within a fixed number of cells in the population.
source: Thus, the increase in levels of SUT650 transcripts in GAL reflects an increase in the number of cells expressing SUT650 and a concomitant decrease in the number of cells expressing HMS2, rather than a change in the levels of transcripts within a fixed number of cells in the population.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA FISH data showing changes in cell populations expressing different transcripts.

claim: The expression of HMS2 and SUT650 is temporally separated.
source: We conclude that the expression of HMS2 and SUT650 is temporally separated, similar to the PHO84 sense and antisense transcripts (Castelnuovo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from FISH data and supported by citation to similar findings at PHO84.

claim: There is potential co-regulation between BAT2 and SUT650.
source: This suggests potential co-regulation between BAT2 and SUT650 and reciprocal regulation of HMS2 and BAT2.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed expression patterns.

claim: There is reciprocal regulation of HMS2 and BAT2.
source: This suggests potential co-regulation between BAT2 and SUT650 and reciprocal regulation of HMS2 and BAT2.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed expression patterns.

claim: There are longer RNA species (C1 and C2) on the HMS2 sense strand extending through the coding region of BAT2 and beyond, consistent with low-level read-through transcripts initiating at the HMS2 promoter.
source: A number of different methods revealed heterogeneity at both the 5′ and 3′ ends of the HMS2 and SUT650 transcripts and longer RNA species (C1 and C2) on the HMS2 sense strand extending through the coding region of BAT2 and beyond, consistent with low-level read-through transcripts initiating at the HMS2 promoter (Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot, 3'RACE, and TIF-seq data.

claim: Read-through transcripts increase upon loss of nuclear exosome (rrp6Δ).
source: These read-through transcripts increase upon loss of nuclear exosome (rrp6Δ) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data comparing WT and rrp6Δ strains.

claim: HMS2 is at the head of a contiguous gene cluster including the downstream genes BAT2 and YJR149W.
source: Thus HMS2 is at the head of a contiguous gene cluster including the downstream genes BAT2 and YJR149W (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcript mapping data showing read-through transcription.

claim: Polyadenylation of HMS2 occurs either 85 nt (proximal) or 426 nt (distal) downstream from the HMS2 stop codon.
source: Polyadenylation (pA) occurs either 85 nt (proximal) or 426 nt (distal) downstream from the HMS2 stop codon.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3'RACE and poly(A) site mapping data.

claim: The distal pA site is 45 nt upstream of the BAT2 initiation codon.
source: The distal pA site is 45 nt upstream of the BAT2 initiation codon, such that this longer transcription event is likely to interfere with initiation of BAT2 transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by mapping of polyadenylation sites relative to gene positions.

claim: The longer HMS2 transcription event is likely to interfere with initiation of BAT2 transcription.
source: The distal pA site is 45 nt upstream of the BAT2 initiation codon, such that this longer transcription event is likely to interfere with initiation of BAT2 transcription.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the proximity of the HMS2 polyadenylation site to the BAT2 promoter.

claim: Additional transcriptional interference might be mediated through the production of the longer HMS2-BAT2 di-cistronic RNA species.
source: Additional transcriptional interference might be mediated through the production of the longer HMS2-BAT2 di-cistronic RNA species.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the mechanism of transcriptional interference.

claim: Insertion of ADH1t efficiently terminates the HMS2 transcript.
source: We confirmed that ADH1t efficiently terminates the HMS2 transcript (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing truncated HMS2 transcript.

claim: There are no detectable transcripts over the HMS2 3′ region when ADH1t is inserted.
source: and that there are no detectable transcripts over the HMS2 3′ region (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data using probes to the 3' region.

claim: The strain with ADH1t inserted showed a ≈twofold increase in BAT2 transcript levels compared to WT in both GLU and GAL.
source: The strain with ADH1t inserted showed a ≈twofold increase in BAT2 transcript levels compared to WT in both GLU and GAL (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot quantitation comparing WT and HMS2:ADH1t strains.

claim: HMS2 sense transcription interferes with BAT2 transcription.
source: We conclude that HMS2 sense transcription interferes with BAT2 transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that blocking HMS2 transcription increases BAT2 levels.

claim: Insertion of the ADH1t into the HMS2 coding region resulted in a ≈fourfold increase in levels of a truncated HMS2 sense transcript (AA).
source: Insertion of the ADH1t into the HMS2 coding region resulted in a ≈fourfold increase in levels of a truncated HMS2 sense transcript (AA) (Figure 3A,B,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot quantitation.

claim: Insertion of ADH1t blocks SUT650 antisense transcription, resulting in the truncated antisense transcript (BA).
source: and blocks SUT650 antisense transcription, resulting in the truncated antisense transcript (BA) (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing truncated antisense transcript.

claim: There are no antisense transcripts over the 5′ region of HMS2 when ADH1t is inserted.
source: We confirm there are no antisense transcripts over the 5′ region of HMS2 (Figure 3B,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data using probes to the 5' region.

claim: In the absence of SUT650, expression of the HMS2:ADH1t transcript remains sensitive to the change in carbon source, showing a similar decrease to full-length HMS2 1 h after transfer from GLU to GAL.
source: In the absence of SUT650, expression of the HMS2:ADH1t transcript remains sensitive to the change in carbon source, showing a similar decrease to full-length HMS2 1 h after transfer from GLU to GAL (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data comparing HMS2 and HMS2:ADH1t in GLU and GAL.

claim: The carbon source responsive signal is received at the HMS2 promoter.
source: This suggests that the carbon source responsive signal is received at the HMS2 promoter and that reciprocal switching of HMS2 and SUT650 is a function of sense transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HMS2:ADH1t remains carbon source responsive without antisense transcription.

claim: Reciprocal switching of HMS2 and SUT650 is a function of sense transcription.
source: This suggests that the carbon source responsive signal is received at the HMS2 promoter and that reciprocal switching of HMS2 and SUT650 is a function of sense transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that blocking antisense doesn't affect carbon source responsiveness.

claim: An increase in the number of HMS2:ADH1t cells containing sense transcript compared to WT was observed when grown in glucose.
source: When grown in glucose, optimal conditions for HMS2 sense transcription, we observed an increase in the number of HMS2:ADH1t cells containing sense transcript compared to WT (Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA FISH analysis.

claim: Antisense transcription acts to limit the number of cells in the population that respond.
source: consistent with a role for antisense transcription in reducing the number of sense transcription initiation events, leading to a decrease in the number of cells in the population that contain the sense transcript. We conclude that SUT650 antisense transcription does not influence the environmental responsiveness of HMS2 transcription but acts to limit the number of cells in the population that respond.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA FISH data showing more cells express HMS2 when antisense is blocked.

claim: SUT650 antisense transcription does not influence the environmental responsiveness of HMS2 transcription.
source: We conclude that SUT650 antisense transcription does not influence the environmental responsiveness of HMS2 transcription but acts to limit the number of cells in the population that respond.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HMS2:ADH1t remains carbon source responsive.

claim: Loss of the antisense transcript (B) occurs when the HMS2 coding region is replaced with URA3.
source: We observed two clear effects. First, loss of the antisense transcript (B), which could be explained either by introduction of a unidirectional terminator in the URA3 ORF coding region or loss of TSSs for SUT650 (Figure 4B–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing absence of antisense transcript in HMS2:URA3 strain.

claim: An increase in the read-through transcripts (C1U) relative to the HMS2:URA3 sense transcript (AU) occurs when the HMS2 coding region is replaced with URA3.
source: Second, an increase in the read-through transcripts (C1U) relative to the HMS2:URA3 sense transcript (AU) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data comparing transcript levels.

claim: Insertion of a terminator (T) at the 3′ region of the HMS2:URA3 hybrid gene results in loss of the read-through transcripts and increased levels of a shorter transcript (AUT).
source: We confirmed these were read-through transcripts by inserting a terminator (T) at the 3′ region of the HMS2:URA3 hybrid gene (Figure 4A) and observing loss of the read-through transcripts and increased levels of a shorter transcript (AUT) (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data comparing HMS2:URA3 and HMS2:URA3:T strains.

claim: Transcripts initiated at the HMS2 promoter remain sensitive to a change in carbon source in the absence of antisense transcription.
source: We note that transcripts initiated at the HMS2 promoter remain sensitive to a change in carbon source in the absence of antisense transcription (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing carbon source regulation in HMS2:URA3 strain.

claim: The increase in the read-through transcript (C1U) relative to the HMS2:URA3 sense transcript (AU) in the absence of antisense transcription suggests a role for antisense transcription in attenuating sense transcription and preventing interference at the BAT2 promoter.
source: The increase in the read-through transcript (C1U) relative to the HMS2:URA3 sense transcript (AU) in the absence of antisense transcription suggests a role for antisense transcription in attenuating sense transcription and preventing interference at the BAT2 promoter.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that loss of antisense increases read-through transcription.

claim: A twofold decrease in BAT2 sense transcript is observed in the antisense-less HMS2:URA3 strain relative to WT in GLU, concomitant with a threefold increase in AU and C1U.
source: Consistent with this, a twofold decrease in BAT2 sense transcript is observed in the antisense-less HMS2:URA3 strain relative to WT in GLU, concomitant with a threefold increase in AU and C1U (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot quantitation comparing WT and HMS2:URA3 strains.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis at the HMS2:BAT2 intergenic region reveals reduced initiation-related modifications (H3K4me3 and H3K56ac) and increased elongation-related modifications (H3K79me3 and H3K36me3) in the HMS2:URA3 hybrid gene.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis at the HMS2:BAT2 intergenic region reveals reduced initiation-related modifications (H3K4me3 and H3K56ac) and increased elongation-related modifications (H3K79me3 and H3K36me3) in the HMS2:URA3 hybrid gene, consistent with transcriptional interference leading to repression of BAT2 transcription initiation (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data comparing histone modifications in WT and HMS2:URA3 strains.

claim: SUT650 antisense transcription changes the proportion of cells expressing HMS2.
source: We conclude that SUT650 antisense transcription (i) changes the proportion of cells expressing HMS2 and (ii) controls the amount of overlapping and read-through transcription from HMS2 and thus levels of BAT2 transcript.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA FISH and Northern blot data.

claim: SUT650 antisense transcription controls the amount of overlapping and read-through transcription from HMS2 and thus levels of BAT2 transcript.
source: We conclude that SUT650 antisense transcription (i) changes the proportion of cells expressing HMS2 and (ii) controls the amount of overlapping and read-through transcription from HMS2 and thus levels of BAT2 transcript.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Northern blot data showing increased read-through and decreased BAT2 when antisense is absent.

claim: At any one time in a single cell, formation of the HMS2 and SUT650 transcription units (TUs) is mutually exclusive.
source: We envisage that at any one time in a single cell, formation of the HMS2 and SUT650 transcription units (TUs) is mutually exclusive, but the formation of the SUT650 TU and the BAT2 TU is not.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the observed data, particularly the lack of co-occurrence of HMS2 and SUT650 nascent transcripts in FISH.

claim: The formation of the SUT650 TU and the BAT2 TU is not mutually exclusive.
source: We envisage that at any one time in a single cell, formation of the HMS2 and SUT650 transcription units (TUs) is mutually exclusive, but the formation of the SUT650 TU and the BAT2 TU is not.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the observed co-regulation of SUT650 and BAT2.

claim: An antisense transcript (BG) is evident in GLU and remains until the sense transcript is induced by GAL in the pGAL1:HMS2 strain.
source: However in the pGAL1:HMS2 strain, an antisense transcript (BG) is evident in GLU and remains until the sense transcript is induced by GAL (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing antisense transcript in pGAL1:HMS2 strain.

claim: Sense transcription represses the antisense transcript.
source: This suggests that sense transcription represses the antisense transcript.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that antisense is present when sense is repressed and disappears when sense is induced.

claim: Removal of Gal4p by treatment with rapamycin for 1 h, after activation of pGAL1:HMS2 for 3 h with GAL, abolishes the HMS2 transcript (AG) and leads to restoration of the antisense transcript (BG).
source: Removal of Gal4p by treatment with rapamycin (Rap) for 1 h, after activation of pGAL1:HMS2 for 3 h with GAL, abolishes the HMS2 transcript (AG) and leads to restoration of the antisense transcript (BG) (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Anchor Away experiment with Northern blot analysis.

claim: The reduction in the antisense transcript is a consequence of sense transcription, rather than the change in condition (GLU to GAL).
source: This confirms that the reduction in the antisense transcript is a consequence of sense transcription, rather than the change in condition (GLU to GAL).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Anchor Away experiment showing antisense restoration when sense is turned off in GAL.

claim: Antisense transcription does not impair sense activation kinetics.
source: No changes in induction rate were apparent, with the sense transcript only detectable after 2 h in both strains, signifying that antisense transcription does not impair sense activation kinetics (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of pGAL1:HMS2 and pGAL1:HMS2:URA3 induction kinetics.

claim: Activation of the pGAL1:HMS2 sense transcript results in up to 3.5-fold repression of BAT2.
source: Activation of the pGAL1:HMS2 sense transcript results in up to 3.5-fold repression of BAT2 (Figure 5F)
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot quantitation of BAT2 levels during pGAL1:HMS2 induction.

claim: pGAL1:HMS2 sense polyadenylation at 426 nt, just upstream of the BAT2 ATG, interferes with BAT2 transcription initiation in galactose.
source: consistent with pGAL1:HMS2 sense polyadenylation at 426 nt, just upstream of the BAT2 ATG, interfering with BAT2 transcription initiation in galactose (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HMS2 induction represses BAT2 and the known polyadenylation site location.

claim: Formation of the HMS2 sense transcription unit represses the formation of the SUT650 and BAT2 transcription units, regardless of conditions.
source: We conclude that formation of the HMS2 sense transcription unit represses the formation of the SUT650 and BAT2 transcription units, regardless of conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing HMS2 transcription represses both SUT650 and BAT2.

claim: There are two species of antisense transcript during induction of pGAL1:HMS2; a long species (BG1), dominant until 30 min after the shift to GAL, and a shorter species (BG2), also detectable after 30 min of growth in GAL and which becomes the dominant antisense transcript form after 1 h.
source: There are two species of antisense transcript during induction of pGAL1:HMS2; a long species (BG1), dominant until 30 min after the shift to GAL, and a shorter species (BG2), also detectable after 30 min of growth in GAL and which becomes the dominant antisense transcript form after 1 h (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing two antisense transcript sizes.

claim: 3′end RACE revealed alternative polyadenylation sites as one cause for the observed size difference, with the long form terminating upstream of the Gal4p binding sites at approx. 500 nt upstream of the ATG in the GAL1 promoter and the shorter form terminating midway through the GAL1 promoter, 195 nt upstream of the GAL1 ATG, and downstream of the Gal4p binding sites.
source: 3′end RACE revealed alternative polyadenylation sites as one cause for the observed size difference, with the long form terminating upstream of the Gal4p binding sites at approx. 500 nt upstream of the ATG in the GAL1 promoter and the shorter form terminating midway through the GAL1 promoter, 195 nt upstream of the GAL1 ATG, and downstream of the Gal4p binding sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3'RACE mapping data.

claim: Upon glucose repression of induced pGAL1:HMS2, levels of the long form of antisense transcript were recovered.
source: Upon glucose repression of induced pGAL1:HMS2, levels of the long form of antisense transcript were recovered (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing antisense recovery after glucose repression.

claim: Antisense transcript shortening after transfer to GAL is an inherent property of the natural SUT650 antisense transcript.
source: Antisense transcript shortening after transfer to GAL is an inherent property of the natural SUT650 antisense transcript (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing SUT650 size changes in WT strain.

claim: Shortening of the antisense transcript is independent of Gal4 binding at pGAL1 and remains for 3 h in GAL in the absence of sense transcription.
source: To ask if this was a function of transcription factor binding to the promoter, we used the pGAL1:HMS2 construct and showed that shortening of the antisense transcript is independent of Gal4 binding at pGAL1 and remains for 3 h in GAL in the absence of sense transcription (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Anchor Away experiment depleting Gal4 while monitoring antisense transcript size.

claim: SUT650 antisense transcription is normally repressed by HMS2 transcription but remains stably expressed in GLU or GAL, varying in the use of polyadenylation sites, when sense transcription is inhibited.
source: We conclude that SUT650 antisense transcription is normally repressed by HMS2 transcription but remains stably expressed in GLU or GAL, varying in the use of polyadenylation sites, when sense transcription is inhibited.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing antisense expression when sense is blocked and alternative polyadenylation in different conditions.

claim: Growth in nutrient-limited GLU-based medium depleted for tryptophan resulted in loss of the HMS2 transcript and accumulation of the short isoform of the SUT650 antisense transcript (B2) in the cbf1Δ and fkh1Δ strains.
source: While under standard growth conditions in GLU these mutant strains showed normal expression of HMS2 and SUT650, growth in nutrient-limited GLU-based medium depleted for tryptophan resulted in loss of the HMS2 transcript and accumulation of the short isoform of the SUT650 antisense transcript (B2) in the cbf1Δ and fkh1Δ strains (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data from transcription factor deletion strains.

claim: The fkh2Δ strain showed reduced levels of SUT650 and increased HMS2 under nutrient-limited growth conditions.
source: In contrast, the fkh2Δ strain showed reduced levels of SUT650 and increased HMS2 under these growth conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data from fkh2Δ strain.

claim: Transcription factors control the balance of sense, and thus antisense transcription, at the HMS2 locus during the cell cycle and during oxidative growth in metabolic cycles.
source: This supports transcription factors controlling the balance of sense, and thus antisense transcription, at this locus during the cell cycle (Fkh factors) (Granovskaia et al., 2010) and during oxidative growth in metabolic cycles (Cbf1) (Tsankov et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of transcription factor deletions and is supported by citations to previous work on these factors.

claim: Transcription factors signal to the HMS2 promoter (Input) to mediate state-changing (antisense-dominant to sense-dominant) in response to environmental conditions.
source: We propose that transcription factors signal to the HMS2 promoter (Input) to mediate state-changing (antisense-dominant to sense-dominant) in response to environmental conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the observed effects of transcription factors on HMS2/SUT650 balance.

claim: Chromatin modulators and components are predominant at RC gene promoters.
source: Of particular interest are the predominance of chromatin modulators and components at RC gene promoters, suggesting that RC promoters are particularly sensitive to chromatin-mediated repression (Tirosh and Barkai, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of factor enrichment at promoters using published data, and is supported by citation.

claim: RC promoters are particularly sensitive to chromatin-mediated repression.
source: Of particular interest are the predominance of chromatin modulators and components at RC gene promoters, suggesting that RC promoters are particularly sensitive to chromatin-mediated repression (Tirosh and Barkai, 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enrichment of chromatin factors at RC promoters and is supported by citation.

claim: Nuclear depletion of TFIIB (Sua7) results in an increase in the HMS2:BAT2 read-through transcript (C).
source: We assessed a role for a number of essential transcription factors using the Anchor Away technique (Haruki et al., 2008) but only upon nuclear depletion of TFIIB (Sua7) did we observe an increase in the HMS2:BAT2 read-through transcript (C) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Anchor Away experiment with Northern blot analysis.

claim: Nuclear depletion of TFIIB results in reduced levels of HMS2 (A), BAT2 (D), and SUT650 (B) transcripts.
source: However, this occurred together with reduced levels of HMS2 (A), BAT2 (D), and SUT650 (B) transcripts, as expected upon depletion of an essential transcription factor.
evidence: The claim is supported by Anchor Away experiment with Northern blot analysis.

claim: The sua7-1 allele results in an increase in HMS2 transcript (A) and sense read-through transcripts (C), coupled with a decrease in the SUT650 antisense transcript (B).
source: Remarkably, we observed an increase in HMS2 transcript (A) and sense read-through transcripts (C), coupled with a decrease in the SUT650 antisense transcript (B) (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data from sua7-1 mutant strain.

claim: TFIIB may have a specific role in determining the antisense transcription unit by establishing directionality of transcription over the region.
source: Thus, TFIIB may have a specific role in determining the antisense transcription unit by establishing directionality of transcription over the region (Tan-Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the sua7-1 phenotype and is supported by citation.

claim: TFIIB aids in sense transcription termination, preventing 'read-through' over the intergenic region between HMS2 and BAT2.
source: For instance, by determining an antisense transcription unit, TFIIB aids in sense transcription termination, preventing 'read-through' over the intergenic region between HMS2 and BAT2.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed increase in read-through in sua7-1 mutant.

claim: In the HMS2:TEF:Kan construct, the SUT650 antisense promoter is functional and produces a truncated antisense transcript (BK) that ends in the vicinity of TEFt.
source: The SUT650 antisense promoter is functional and produces a truncated antisense transcript (BK) that ends in the vicinity of TEFt (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data from the engineered strain.

claim: TEFt functions bi-directionally to terminate SUT650 (BK), the sense transcript from pTEF expressing the kanamycin resistance (KanMX) transcript (K), and the sense transcript (AK) initiated at the HMS2 promoter.
source: Thus TEFt functions bi-directionally to terminate SUT650 (BK), the sense transcript from pTEF, expressing the kanamycin resistance (KanMX) transcript (K), and the sense transcript (AK) initiated at the HMS2 promoter and terminating at TEFt (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from Northern blot data showing multiple transcripts terminating at TEFt.

claim: pTEF produces an antisense transcript (E) extending into pHMS2.
source: pTEF is a well-characterised (Steiner and Philippsen, 1994) strong bi-directional promoter and produces an antisense transcript (E) extending into pHMS2.
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data and citation to characterization of pTEF.

claim: Insertion of ADH1t directly upstream of pTEF resulted in increased levels of a truncated sense transcript (AA) and considerably reduced levels of antisense transcript (E).
source: To confirm this, we inserted ADH1t directly upstream of pTEF (Figure 7A). This resulted in increased levels of a truncated sense transcript (AA) and considerably reduced levels of antisense transcript (E) (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data comparing HMS2:TEF:Kan and HMS2:ADH1t:TEF:Kan strains.

claim: The pTEF.KanMX.TEFt expression cassette is strongly expressed, effectively preventing the formation of the HMS2:SUT650 transcription units.
source: We suggest that the pTEF.KanMX.TEFt expression cassette is strongly expressed (compare levels of transcripts AK and K in Figure 7E), effectively preventing the formation of the HMS2:SUT650 transcription units.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Northern blot data showing high expression of the cassette and loss of HMS2/SUT650 TUs.

claim: When the TEF promoter is disabled, reducing expression of the pTEF.KanMX.TEFt expression cassette, the SUT650 antisense transcription unit can form, resulting in the appearance of the long antisense transcript.
source: When the TEF promoter is disabled, reducing expression of the pTEF.KanMX.TEFt expression cassette, the SUT650 antisense transcription unit can form, resulting in the appearance of the long antisense transcript.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Northern blot data showing long antisense transcript in TEFdel mutant.

claim: A long deletion (HMS2.TEFdel1:Kan), removing all the TEF promoter sequences upstream of the TATA box, results in a significant reduction in expression of the KanMX cassette itself (transcript K) and in levels of the antisense transcript (E).
source: A long deletion (HMS2.TEFdel1:Kan), removing all the TEF promoter sequences upstream of the TATA box, results in a significant reduction in expression of the KanMX cassette itself (transcript K) and in levels of the antisense transcript (E) (Figure 7D,E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data from TEFdel1 mutant strain.

claim: In the HMS2.TEFdel1:Kan strain, a new antisense transcript from the 3′ end of HMS2 that reads through TEFt (BpTEFdel) was observed.
source: Remarkably, in this strain, we observed a new antisense transcript from the 3′ end of HMS2 that reads through TEFt (BpTEFdel) (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing a long antisense transcript in TEFdel1 mutant.

claim: The disabled weak pTEFdel1 resulted in reduced functionality at TEFt allowing BpTEFdel, initiating at the SUT650 antisense promoter, to read through TEFt, the KanMX cassette and into the HMS2 promoter.
source: Thus, the disabled weak pTEFdel1 resulted in reduced functionality at TEFt allowing BpTEFdel, initiating at the SUT650 antisense promoter, to read through TEFt, the KanMX cassette and into the HMS2 promoter (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that weakening pTEF allows antisense read-through of TEFt.

claim: The experiment illustrates the conditional nature of the bi-directional TEF terminator.
source: This experiment illustrates (i) the conditional nature of the bi-directional TEF terminator and (ii) the remarkable plasticity of interleaved transcription units.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TEFt function depends on promoter strength.

claim: The experiment illustrates the remarkable plasticity of interleaved transcription units.
source: This experiment illustrates (i) the conditional nature of the bi-directional TEF terminator and (ii) the remarkable plasticity of interleaved transcription units.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different transcription units can form depending on promoter/terminator strength.

claim: Overlapping transcription, in both the sense and antisense orientations, constitutes an additional layer of regulation at clustered genes by managing state-switching in response to environmental change.
source: Here we show that overlapping transcription, in both the sense and antisense orientations, constitutes an additional layer of regulation at clustered genes by managing state-switching in response to environmental change.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Transcription in the HMS2 sense orientation transmits the state-defining regulatory signals to neighbouring genes through mechanisms of cis-acting transcriptional interference, thus repressing BAT2, YJR149W, and SUT650.
source: We propose that transcription in the HMS2 sense orientation transmits the state-defining regulatory signals to neighbouring genes through mechanisms of cis-acting transcriptional interference, thus repressing BAT2, YJR149W, and SUT650.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the experimental observations of transcriptional interference.

claim: The HMS2:BAT2 cluster is conserved in a range of yeast strains expected of a functional linkage.
source: Moreover, the HMS2:BAT2 cluster is conserved in a range of yeast strains expected of a functional linkage.
evidence: The claim is based on evolutionary conservation analysis.

claim: There are many loci at which di-cistronic read-through transcripts are evident.
source: There are many loci at which di-cistronic read-through transcripts are evident (Pelechano et al., 2013), raising the possibility that transcriptional interference leading to reciprocal expression of genes in tandem arrays is a much more widespread phenomenon in yeast.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published TIF-seq data.

claim: Transcriptional interference leading to reciprocal expression of genes in tandem arrays may be a widespread phenomenon in yeast.
source: There are many loci at which di-cistronic read-through transcripts are evident (Pelechano et al., 2013), raising the possibility that transcriptional interference leading to reciprocal expression of genes in tandem arrays is a much more widespread phenomenon in yeast.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the prevalence of di-cistronic transcripts and the findings at HMS2:BAT2.

claim: The capacity of a terminator to function is conditional on the strength of the proximal promoter.
source: This work indicates the capacity of a terminator to function is conditional on the strength of the proximal promoter.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the engineering experiments showing terminator read-through depends on promoter strength.

claim: Stronger promoters preferentially select the proximal terminator.
source: We suggest that this reflects the role for promoters in defining the beginnings and ends of TUs (El Kaderi et al., 2009; O'Sullivan et al., 2004); stronger promoters preferentially selecting the proximal terminator.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed relationship between promoter strength and terminator usage, supported by citations.

claim: The sua7-1 allele is associated specifically with the 3′ region of genes, polyadenylation/transcription termination and higher order structures (gene loops) in chromatin.
source: To explore this further, we used a well-characterised allele of SUA7 (sua7-1) (E62K) (Pinto et al., 1994), associated specifically with the 3′ region of genes, polyadenylation/transcription termination and higher order structures (gene loops) in chromatin (Medler et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous characterization of the sua7-1 allele.

claim: Overlapping transcription and the formation of alternative transcription units, associated with temporally segregated gene expression, will be a general feature of gene regulation.
source: We suggest that overlapping transcription and the formation of alternative transcription units, associated with temporally segregated gene expression, will be a general feature of gene regulation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis extrapolating from the findings at HMS2:BAT2 to genome-wide regulation.
